newsitem.title: USA: Iowa hog plant cutbacks may point to new trend.
newsitem.headline: Iowa hog plant cutbacks may point to new trend.

text.p: Iowa has long been the pork capital of the U.S. but recent migration of hog farms to regions outside the Midwest in search of better political and temperate climates may soon raise challenges to that title.
"The hog is out of the pen and he is heading south," said George Dahlman, agriculture analyst with Piper Jaffrey Inc.
The trend toward a shrinking Midwest hog herd made headlines this week when IBP Inc, one of the nation's largest pork packers, said it was cutting production at two Iowa slaughter plants.
IBP, in explaining the cutbacks, cited migration of hog production out of Iowa that has left too few hogs to fully utilize the plants.

Hog populations have steadily increased in the 1990s in North Carolina, Oklahoma, Arkansas and Utah. These states, said Dahlman, offer producers less restrictive regulations, more open ground and more moderate weather than Iowa.

IBP spokesman Gary Mickelson said Thursday the company currently does not have plans to operate a plant in the south, but if the migration continues, packing companies will have to locate plants "where the supply is."
"I think they are playing a wait-and-see game," said John Lawrence, a livestock economist at Iowa State University. "It may be better to ship hogs to Iowa rather than build a plant."
According to the Livestock Marketing Information Center in Denver, from 1987 to 1996 the number of market hogs in Iowa fell by 1.7 million head to about 12.2 million.
Iowa still raised about 22 percent of the 56 million U.S. hogs in 1996, but that was down from 25.6 percent in 1987.
Over the same '87-'96 period, the hog herd in traditionally key Illinois shrunk by 800,000, Indiana by 635,000 and Ohio numbers fell 520,000.
Meanwhile, hog numbers in North Carolina soared by 6.04 million head, Arkansas by 311,000, Oklahoma by 980,000, Missouri by 485,000, Colorado 324,000 and Utah by 97,000.
Aside from Missouri, Minnesota was the only other Midwest state with a rise in hog numbers, up 395,000 in that period.
Livestock industry sources said Iowa's laws and population have turned hostile toward hog operations.

Iowa's Secretary of Agriculture Dale Cochran said IBP may be unfairly blaming the state. One of the industry's problems is that there has been excess hog slaughter capacity in Iowa since 1986, he said.

A recent Des Moines Register newspaper article said residents of Maple Grove, Iowa, put a trailer home near the site of a proposed hog farm, which some industry sources said was clearly done to prevent the construction of the hog farm.
The placement of the trailer, which would have been closer to the hog buildings than state laws allow, led to the Iowa Department of Natural Resources' denial of a building permit for the farm.
"We don't have any stricter rules than anybody else," Cochran told Reuters.
Cochran said the state is working on legislation that will allow for the co-existence of large and small hog operations with residents and still comply with environmental rules.
Reflecting its traditional dominance in hog output, Iowa is still home to 12 large pork packing plants. So the concern is that IBP's move may signal other processors to follow.
Spokespersons for ConAgra and Excel Inc, a division of Cargill Inc, said they have no plans now to operate plants in the south or move from their Iowa locations.
But some packing company sources said their Midwest plants already ship hogs in from Arkansas, Texas, Georgia and North Carolina.
Iowa State's Lawrence said over the longer term, he sees hog breeding operations concentrating in southern states but production of slaughter hogs may stay largely in the Midwest.
"I still believe we will be a finishing state but I have a concern whether we will have any sows left," he said.
((Bob Burgdorfer, 312-408-8720))
